User.description: Represents a user in the Cinepedia application.

id.description: Unique identifier for the User entity.

creationTimestamp.description: Timestamp of when the user account was created.

trustScore.description: A score representing the user's trustworthiness based on account age and review history.

Movie.title: Movie
Movie.description: Represents a movie in the Cinepedia application.

id.description: Unique identifier for the Movie entity.

synopsis.description: Synopsis or summary of the movie's plot.

imageUrl.description: URL of the movie's poster image.

Review.title: Review
Review.description: Represents a user's review of a movie.

id.description: Unique identifier for the Review entity.

timestamp.description: Timestamp of when the review was submitted.

likes.description: The number of likes the review has received.

Poll.description: Represents a movie poll where users can vote between two movies.

id.description: Unique identifier for the Poll entity.

movie1Id.description: Reference to Movie. First movie in the poll.

movie2Id.description: Reference to Movie. Second movie in the poll.

startTime.description: Timestamp of when the poll started.

endTime.description: Timestamp of when the poll ends.

Vote.title: Vote
Vote.description: Represents a user's vote in a movie poll.

id.description: Unique identifier for the Vote entity.

movieId.description: Reference to Movie. The movie the user voted for.

timestamp.description: Timestamp of when the vote was cast.

firestore.reasoning:
The Firestore structure is designed to prioritize authorization independence, clarity, and scalability. It leverages denormalization to avoid hierarchical authorization dependencies, ensuring atomic operations and simplified security rules. Segregation of data into collections with homogeneous security postures simplifies rules and ensures QAPs. Path-based ownership is used where appropriate to avoid complex authorization logic, and membership maps are employed for collaborative data access. Radically consistent naming conventions improve debuggability.

Specifically, authorization independence is achieved by denormalizing user information (isEmailVerified, trustScore) into the reviews collection. This allows us to write security rules for reviews without needing to perform `get()` operations to the users collection. This is crucial for maintaining atomic operations (transactions and batches) when creating or updating reviews.

The design supports QAPs as follows:

*   Secure List Operations: By segregating data based on ownership (e.g., `/users/{userId}/reviews`) and using dedicated collections for global roles (`/roles_admin/{uid}` - although not explicitly used here, it's a general principle), the structure ensures that list operations can be secured without filtering data based on content.
*   Membership Model: The `members` field in collaborative documents is denormalized, which avoids `get()` calls to parent documents to verify membership, allowing secure reads and writes without complex filtering.
